examples.en: I'm so upset because my friend looks down on me.
You shouldn't look down on people because of their appearance.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 가난하다고 괄시한 친구를 다시 만났어요.
examples.en: I met again a friend who looked down on me for being poor when we were kids.

examples.ko: 그는 같은 학교 후배를 너무 괄시했어요.
examples.en: He treated his junior from the same school with too much contempt.

examples.ko: 손님을 괄시하는 가게에는 다시 가고 싶지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't want to go back to a shop that treats customers with contempt.
Please don't look down on the children.

explain: '무시하다'보다 사람을 낮춰 보고 차갑게 대한다는 느낌이 강해요. 주로 사람을 대할 때 쓰고, 비슷한 말로 '업신여기다', 반대로 잘 대하는 건 '대접하다'라고 해요. '푸대접하다'는 대접을 소홀히 한다는 쪽에 더 가까워요.
explain_en: It feels stronger than '무시하다': you look down on someone and treat them coldly. It is mostly used for how you treat people. A similar word is '업신여기다', and the opposite is '대접하다' (to treat well). '푸대접하다' leans more toward treating someone carelessly.

examples.en: I had my puppy get a rabies shot.

examples.ko: 광견병은 동물에게 물려서 걸릴 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can catch rabies from an animal bite.

examples.ko: 해외여행 가기 전에 광견병 백신을 맞았어요.
examples.en: I got a rabies vaccine before traveling abroad.
A dog with rabies starts acting strangely.
There is almost no rabies in this country.

examples.ko: 길고양이에게 물렸으면 광견병 검사를 받아 보세요.
examples.en: If a stray cat bit you, get tested for rabies.

explain: '광견병에 걸리다', '광견병 예방접종'처럼 자주 말해요. 개에게 물렸다는 이야기와 함께 나오는 일이 많아요. 사람이 걸린 병은 '공수병'이라고도 해요.
explain_en: Common patterns are '광견병에 걸리다' (catch rabies) and '광견병 예방접종' (rabies vaccination). It often comes up when someone was bitten by a dog. The disease in humans is also called '공수병'.

examples.en: I found a used car in the newspaper ad section.
I put news about our shop in the ad column.
My father reads the ad column first every morning.
This magazine has too many ad sections.
I found a part-time job by looking at the ad column.
The job ad column changes every Monday.

explain: 신문이나 잡지에서 광고를 싣는 자리를 말해요. '-란'은 칸이나 지면을 뜻해서 '댓글란', '메모란'처럼 다른 말에도 붙어요. 요즘은 인터넷 광고가 많아서 종이 신문 이야기에 주로 나와요.
explain_en: It refers to the place in a newspaper or magazine where ads are printed. The suffix '-란' means a column or space, as in '댓글란' (comment section) and '메모란' (memo field). Today online ads are common, so this word mostly appears when talking about paper newspapers.

examples.en: I polished my shoes until they shone.
The newly laid floor is shiny.
The car got glossy after I applied wax.
I feel good wearing shiny shoes.
I wiped the floor hard until it gleamed.

examples.ko: 구두가 광나지 않아서 다시 닦아야 해요.
examples.en: My shoes aren't shiny, so I have to polish them again.

explain: '광이 나다'와 같은 뜻이고, 구두·바닥·자동차처럼 닦아서 윤이 나는 물건에 많이 써요. 저절로 반짝이는 상태를 말하고, 사람이 일부러 반짝이게 하는 건 '광내다'예요.
explain_en: It means the same as '광이 나다' and is often used for things that gleam after being wiped, such as shoes, floors and cars. It describes the state of shining; when a person deliberately makes something shine, use '광내다'.

examples.en: I polished my shoes and went to the interview.
I bought wax to polish my car on the weekend.
My father polishes his shoes every day.

examples.ko: 마루를 광낼 때는 마른 걸레를 쓰세요.
examples.en: Use a dry cloth when you polish the floor.
I have a date today, so I shined my shoes.

examples.ko: 바빠서 구두를 광내지 않고 그냥 나왔어요.
examples.en: I was busy, so I left without polishing my shoes.

explain: '광나다'는 저절로 반짝이는 상태이고, '광내다'는 사람이 닦아서 일부러 반짝이게 하는 거예요. 둘은 짝처럼 같이 알아 두면 좋아요. 구두, 마루, 차처럼 닦을 수 있는 물건에 써요.
explain_en: '광나다' describes something shining by itself, while '광내다' means a person deliberately makes it shine by rubbing. It helps to learn them as a pair. It is used for things you can wipe or buff, like shoes, floors and cars.

examples.en: They found a gold vein in the mountains.
I heard there is a large mineral vein in this area.
A mineral vein runs long underground.
Copper came out of the new vein.

examples.ko: 광맥까지 파 내려가는 데 몇 달이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: It took months to dig down to the vein.
People wandered the mountains looking for a vein of ore.

explain: 광석이 줄기처럼 길게 모여 묻혀 있는 곳을 말해요. '금광맥', '철광맥'처럼 앞에 광물 이름을 붙여 쓰기도 해요. 보통 '광맥을 찾다', '광맥을 발견하다'로 말해요.
explain_en: It is a place where ore lies buried in a long, stream-like line. You can put a mineral name before it, as in '금광맥' (gold vein) and '철광맥' (iron vein). The usual patterns are '광맥을 찾다' and '광맥을 발견하다'.

examples.ko: 이 생수에는 광물질이 많이 들어 있어요.
examples.en: This bottled water contains a lot of minerals.
Minerals are important for bone health.
Plants get minerals from the soil.

examples.ko: 이 화장품에는 광물질 성분이 들어 있어요.
examples.en: This cosmetic contains mineral ingredients.

examples.ko: 비타민뿐만 아니라 광물질도 꼭 챙겨 드세요.
examples.en: Make sure to take minerals as well as vitamins.
It's a paint made with color taken from minerals.

explain: 땅이나 돌에서 나오는 무기물을 말해요. 영양 이야기에서는 '미네랄'이라고 더 많이 해요. '광물질'은 설명하는 글이나 수업에서 자주 보여요.
explain_en: It refers to inorganic substances that come from the earth or rocks. In talk about nutrition, people more often say '미네랄'. '광물질' appears more in explanatory texts and classes.

examples.en: He shows a frantic level of interest in baseball.
Fanatical fans gathered in front of the concert hall.
My younger brother is obsessively into games.
That person's hobby is a bit obsessive.

examples.ko: 광적일 만큼 책을 모으는 친구가 있어요.
examples.en: I have a friend who collects books almost obsessively.
I was surprised because the cheering was so frenzied.

explain: '광적인', '광적으로', '광적이다'처럼 써요. 좋아하는 마음이 정상을 넘었다는 느낌이라 칭찬보다는 놀라거나 걱정하는 말투에 가까워요. '열광적'은 뜨겁게 환호하는 느낌이 더 강해요.
explain_en: It is used as '광적인', '광적으로' or '광적이다'. It suggests that someone's enthusiasm goes beyond normal, so it sounds more surprised or worried than praising. '열광적' puts more emphasis on hot, cheering excitement.

examples.en: Grandmother put the wild greens in a basket.
She carries a basket on her head to the market.
I picked a basketful of apples.
This basket is made of bamboo.
I took a piece of bread out of the basket.
The basket was too heavy, so we lifted it together.

explain: 대나무나 싸리 같은 것으로 엮은 둥글고 큰 바구니예요. 요즘 일상에서는 보통 '바구니'라고 하고, '광주리'는 옛날 시장이나 시골 장면에서 자주 나와요.
explain_en: It is a large round basket woven from bamboo or similar material. In daily life today people usually say '바구니', while '광주리' often appears in scenes of old markets or the countryside.

examples.en: I applied polish to my shoes and wiped them.
This polish doesn't smell strong.
Thanks to the polish, the floor sparkles.

examples.ko: 광택제가 다 떨어져서 새로 사야 해요.
examples.en: The polish ran out, so I have to buy more.
Try rubbing small scratches with polish.
Even without polish, a dry towel is enough.

explain: 물건 표면을 반짝이게 하려고 바르는 약품이에요. 구두, 자동차, 가구에 쓰는 종류가 달라서 보통 '구두 광택제'처럼 앞에 대상을 붙여요. 이 약품으로 닦는 행동은 '광내다'로 말해요.
explain_en: It is a product applied to make a surface shine. Different kinds exist for shoes, cars and furniture, so people usually put the object before it, as in '구두 광택제'. The action of polishing with it is '광내다'.

examples.ko: 밤새 광풍이 불어서 잠을 못 잤어요.
examples.en: A violent wind blew all night, so I couldn't sleep.
The roof was blown away by the fierce wind.
The boats came back to port to avoid the storm winds.
The fierce wind didn't die down until dawn.

examples.ko: 부동산 광풍 속에서 집값이 크게 올랐어요.
examples.en: Housing prices rose sharply amid the property frenzy.
That song swept across the country like a storm.

explain: 몹시 사납게 부는 바람이에요. 일상에서 바람이 센 날은 '강풍'이나 '바람이 세다'라고 하고, '광풍'은 더 거칠고 글 같은 느낌이에요. 뉴스에서는 '투자 광풍'처럼 사회가 한쪽으로 휩쓸리는 모습을 비유할 때도 써요.
explain_en: It means a wind that blows extremely fiercely. In daily life people say '강풍' or '바람이 세다' for a windy day, while '광풍' sounds rougher and more literary. In the news it is also used figuratively, as in '투자 광풍' (investment frenzy), when society gets swept in one direction.

en: for no reason; needlessly; without cause

examples.en: It's raining, so I feel lonely for no reason.
I felt good for no particular reason since morning.

examples.ko: 괜스레 그 사람 생각이 나서 전화했어요.
examples.en: I thought of that person for no reason and called.
Tears came for no reason, so I looked up at the sky.
I brought it up needlessly and it turned into a fight.

examples.ko: 시험 결과가 나오기 전에는 괜스레 불안해요.
examples.en: Before the exam results come out, I feel uneasy without knowing why.

explain: '괜히'와 뜻이 거의 같지만, 말할 때는 '괜히'를 훨씬 많이 쓰고 '괜스레'는 글이나 노랫말 같은 느낌이 있어요. 이유 없이 어떤 기분이 든다는 뜻으로도, 안 해도 될 일을 해서 결과가 안 좋다는 뜻으로도 써요.
explain_en: It means almost the same as '괜히', but in speech '괜히' is used much more, while '괜스레' feels more like writing or song lyrics. It can mean feeling something for no reason, or doing something unnecessary that turns out badly.

examples.en: My father tills the field with a hoe.
I went out to the garden plot carrying a hoe.

examples.ko: 괭이가 무뎌서 흙이 잘 안 파져요.
examples.en: The hoe is dull, so the soil doesn't dig well.
I washed the soil off the hoe with water.
The hoe handle broke, so I bought a new one.

examples.ko: 이 괭이는 날이 넓어서 쓰기 편해요.
examples.en: This hoe has a wide blade, so it's easy to use.

explain: 밭을 파고 일구는 농기구예요. 작은 '호미'는 쪼그려 앉아 잡초를 매는 데 쓰고, 괭이는 서서 흙을 크게 파는 데 써서 쓰임이 달라요. 도시에서는 텃밭이나 농촌 이야기에서 만나는 말이에요.
explain_en: It is a farm tool used to dig and break up soil. A small '호미' is used while squatting to weed, whereas a 괭이 is used standing to dig soil in bigger strokes. In cities you mostly meet the word in talk about garden plots or the countryside.
